```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.6, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%",
                      dev = if (requireNamespace("svglite", quietly = TRUE)) "svglite" else
                        if (isTRUE(capabilities("cairo"))) "svg" else "png")
library(Rcausality)
# Long-running results are precomputed and shipped in vignettes/precomputed/;
# the code shown is exactly the code that produced them.
# Sys.setenv(RCAUSALITY_RECOMPUTE = "true") recomputes everything.
.pre <- function(name, expr) {
  f <- file.path("precomputed", paste0(name, ".rds"))
  if (file.exists(f) && !identical(Sys.getenv("RCAUSALITY_RECOMPUTE"), "true")) return(readRDS(f))
  v <- expr
  dir.create("precomputed", showWarnings = FALSE)
  saveRDS(v, f, compress = "xz")
  v
}
has_ranger <- requireNamespace("ranger", quietly = TRUE)
```

# Overview

The classical Granger test regresses the effect on its own past and on the
past of the cause in a stationary linear autoregression, with enough
observations for the F-test. This vignette shows the tools of
**Rcausality** for the situations where one of these assumptions fails, and
for checking and using the detected links.

| Situation | Tool | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| integrated or cointegrated series | `rcausality(method = "toda_yamamoto")` | Toda & Yamamoto (1995) |
| causality at some frequencies only | `granger_spectral()` | Geweke (1982); Breitung & Candelon (2006) |
| nonlinear dependence | `rcausality(method = "diks_panchenko")`, `diks_panchenko()` | Diks & Panchenko (2006) |
| nonlinear, machine learning | `rcausality(method = "rf_granger")`, `rf_granger()` | Kosztyán, Mátrai & Kiss (2026) |
| short series | `bayes_control(prior = "minnesota")` | Litterman (1986); Giannone, Lenza & Primiceri (2015) |
| many short series (panels) | `panel_granger()` | Dumitrescu & Hurlin (2012) |
| are the links artefacts? | `placebo_test()`, `robustness()`, `compare_methods()` | Theiler et al. (1992); Haufe et al. (2013) |
| do the links help forecasting? | `predict()`, `forecast_causal()`, `forecast_compare()` | Diebold & Mariano (1995) |

All of these run in parallel (`cores`), with results that do not depend on
the number of cores (see `?Rcausality-parallel` and the last section).

# Integrated series: the Toda-Yamamoto test

For integrated series the Wald statistic of the levels VAR has a
nonstandard distribution. Toda and Yamamoto (1995) add `d_max` extra lags
(the maximal order of integration) that are estimated but not tested; the
Wald test of the first `p` lags is then asymptotically chi-squared whatever
the integration and cointegration properties, so no unit-root pre-test is
needed.

```{r ty}
set.seed(1); n <- 300
x <- cumsum(rnorm(n))                                 # a random walk
y <- numeric(n); for (t in 3:n) y[t] <- y[t - 1] + 0.6 * (x[t - 1] - x[t - 2]) + rnorm(1)
r_ty <- rcausality(x, y, method = "toda_yamamoto", method_args = list(d_max = 1))
r_ty$pairs[, c("cause", "effect", "lag", "statistic", "df1", "df2", "p_value", "significant")]
```

# Causality in the frequency domain

Geweke (1982) decomposed the predictive gain over the frequencies; the
average of the spectral measure equals the time-domain measure
`log(RSS_restricted / RSS_full)`. Breitung and Candelon (2006) test the
absence of causality at a frequency `w` by two linear restrictions on the
cause's coefficients. When `x` enters as the sum of its last two values,
`0.4 (x[t-1] + x[t-2])`, the transfer of `x` to `y` has the gain
`0.8 |cos(w / 2)|`: it is largest in the long run (low frequencies) and
vanishes at the period of two time units:

```{r spectral, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "Spectral Granger causality. Top: Geweke's measure per frequency (dotted: the time-domain measure). Bottom: pointwise Breitung-Candelon tests; shaded: frequency bands with causality at the 5 % level."}
set.seed(2); n <- 600; x <- rnorm(n); y <- numeric(n)
for (t in 3:n) y[t] <- 0.3 * y[t - 1] + 0.4 * (x[t - 1] + x[t - 2]) + rnorm(1)
gs <- granger_spectral(x, y, lag = 3)
gs
plot(gs)
```

The tests are pointwise: with 256 frequencies an isolated rejection (such
as the single frequency of `y -> x` above) is expected by chance; bands of
consecutive rejections carry the evidence.

# Nonlinear causality

## The Diks-Panchenko test

The nonparametric test of Diks and Panchenko (2006) compares the joint
density of (cause's past, effect's past, effect's present) with the
product implied by conditional independence, with box kernels of bandwidth
`eps` (default `min(1.5, 8 n^(-2/7))` standard deviations). Two logistic
maps coupled through the map function are a textbook case where linear
correlations are weak:

```{r dp}
lg <- sim_logistic(500, "x_to_y", seed = 1)
rcausality(lg, method = "granger")$classes[, c("var1", "var2", "class")]
r_dp <- rcausality(lg, method = "diks_panchenko")
r_dp$pairs[, c("cause", "effect", "statistic", "effect_size", "p_value", "significant")]
```

`effect_size` is the standardised statistic `sqrt(n) T_n / S_n`. With
`method_args = list(filter = "var")` the test is applied to the residuals
of a VAR, so that only the nonlinear part of the dependence is tested.

## Random-forest Granger-like causality

The approach of Kosztyán, Mátrai and Kiss (2026) keeps Granger's
predictive definition but replaces the linear regression by a random
forest. The out-of-bag gain `1 - MSE(own + cause) / MSE(own)` is tested
against circular-shift surrogates of the cause; the honest rolling-origin
out-of-sample gain, the permutation importance of the cause's lags and a
shadow-feature rule (the cause must beat a shifted copy of itself) are
reported with it.

```{r rf, eval = has_ranger}
r_rf <- .pre("ext-rf", rcausality(lg, method = "rf_granger", lag = 1, n_perm = 99, seed = 1,
                                  method_args = list(num_trees = 200, folds = 5)))
r_rf$pairs[, c("cause", "effect", "statistic", "p_value", "significant")]
r_rf$extra[, c("cause", "effect", "oob_gain", "oos_gain", "vi_cause", "shadow_hit")]
```

A non-positive gain gives `p = 1`: in coupled deterministic systems the
driven series carries information about its driver, and a test of
*dependence* would also flag the reverse direction; Granger's definition
asks for an *improvement* of the prediction.

# Short series: the hierarchical Minnesota prior

With `K` series and lag `p` the unrestricted regression has `1 + K p`
coefficients. For short series the F-test has few residual degrees of
freedom, loses power, or cannot be computed at all, and the BIC
approximation of the Bayes factor is unreliable. The Minnesota prior
(Litterman 1986) shrinks every coefficient towards zero, more strongly for
distant lags; its overall tightness `lambda` is integrated out under the
Gamma hyperprior of Giannone, Lenza and Primiceri (2015). The Bayes factor

$$\mathrm{BF}_{10} = \frac{\int p(y \mid \text{cause lags in}, \lambda)\, p(\lambda)\, d\lambda}{\int p(y \mid \text{cause lags out}, \lambda)\, p(\lambda)\, d\lambda}$$

is a ratio of closed-form normal-inverse-gamma marginal likelihoods
averaged over a grid of `lambda`, and exact posterior draws follow from the
same grid.

```{r minn}
d14 <- sim_var(14, n_series = 3, seed = 6)       # 14 observations, 3 series
r_m <- rcausality(d14, conditional = TRUE, lag = 3, method = "bayes_granger", prior = "minnesota",
                  control = bayes_control(n_iter = 500), seed = 1)
r_m$pairs[, c("cause", "effect", "lag", "bf10", "post_prob", "evidence")]
```

The F-test of the conditional lag-3 model is not available (13
coefficients for 11 observations; the frequentist run behind the table had
to shorten the lag to 2), while the Bayesian comparison uses the requested
order and grades the evidence, for and against.

The simulation below repeats, for every sample size, 300 conditional tests
of `x -> y` in a four-series VAR(1) (coupling 0.4 for the power, 0 for the
false-positive rate; lag 2, so the unrestricted model has 9 coefficients).

```{r minn-sim}
sim_short <- function(n, coupling) {
  B <- diag(0.5, 4); B[2, 1] <- coupling; B[3, 4] <- 0.3
  X <- matrix(0, n + 100, 4); E <- matrix(rnorm((n + 100) * 4), n + 100)
  for (t in 2:(n + 100)) X[t, ] <- B %*% X[t - 1, ] + E[t, ]
  X <- X[-(1:100), ]; colnames(X) <- c("x", "y", "z1", "z2")
  g <- rcausality(X[, 1], X[, 2:4], directions = "forward", conditional = TRUE, lag = 2)$pairs[1, ]
  bic <- rcausality(X[, 1], X[, 2:4], directions = "forward", conditional = TRUE, lag = 2,
                    method = "bayes_granger", prior = "bic")$pairs$bf10[1]
  m <- bayes_granger(X[, 2], X[, 1], X[, 3:4], lag = 2,
                     control = bayes_control(prior = "minnesota", n_iter = 4, chains = 1))
  c(`F-test (p < 0.05)` = isTRUE(g$p_value < 0.05), `BIC Bayes factor > 3` = isTRUE(bic > 3),
    `Minnesota Bayes factor > 3` = m$bf10 > 3)
}
short <- .pre("ext-short", {
  set.seed(1)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c(15, 20, 30, 50, 100), function(n) {
    pw <- rowMeans(replicate(300, sim_short(n, 0.4))); fp <- rowMeans(replicate(300, sim_short(n, 0)))
    data.frame(n = n, rule = names(pw), power = pw, false_positive = fp, row.names = NULL)
  }))
})
```

```{r minn-plot, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Short series, conditional test in a four-series VAR: power (left) and false-positive rate (right) of the F-test, the BIC Bayes factor and the hierarchical Minnesota Bayes factor."}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2.5, 1))
cols <- c("#555555", "#B2403A", "#2B5C8A"); rules <- unique(short$rule)
for (what in c("power", "false_positive")) {
  plot(NA, xlim = range(short$n), ylim = if (what == "power") c(0, 1) else c(0, 0.4), log = "x",
       xlab = "series length n", ylab = if (what == "power") "power" else "false-positive rate",
       main = if (what == "power") "Power (coupling 0.4)" else "False positives (no coupling)", font.main = 2, cex.main = 0.9)
  if (what != "power") abline(h = 0.05, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
  for (i in seq_along(rules)) { s <- short[short$rule == rules[i], ]; lines(s$n, s[[what]], col = cols[i], lwd = 2, type = "b", pch = 16) }
  if (what == "power") legend("bottomright", rules, col = cols, lwd = 2, pch = 16, bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
}
par(op)
```

The Minnesota Bayes factor keeps the false-positive rate near the nominal
level of the F-test while its power for the shortest series is about twice
that of the F-test; the BIC approximation, by contrast, declares spurious
links in short samples.

# Panels of short series

`panel_granger()` triangulates the evidence of many short series:
unit-level tests with false-discovery-rate control, the Dumitrescu-Hurlin
test for heterogeneous panels (exact finite-T moments), the pooled
fixed-effects test, the pooled Bayes factor (Minnesota prior by default),
and the pooled random-forest test; `n_placebo` adds the placebo
distribution of every pooled statistic (within-unit circular shifts).

```{r panel, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Unit-level evidence: every point is one unit; the labels give the decisions of the panel procedures (+ = link)."}
pd <- sim_panel(n_units = 30, n_time = 15, scenario = "x_to_y", seed = 1)
pg <- .pre("ext-panel", panel_granger(pd, id = "unit", time = "time", methods = c("units", "dh", "pooled", "bayes"),
                                      n_placebo = 199, seed = 1))
pg
plot(pg)
```

No unit shows the link on its own after the false-discovery-rate
correction (15 observations each), while the Dumitrescu-Hurlin test and the
pooled procedures find it, and the placebo p-values confirm that the
pooled statistics are far outside what shifted causes produce. In the
reverse direction the pooled Bayes factor is evidence *against* a link.

# Are the links artefacts? Placebo, time reversal, robustness, triangulation

```{r placebo, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Left: number of links in placebo data (independent circular shifts of every series; red: the data). Right: evidence and placebo p-value of every link."}
d3 <- sim_var(300, n_series = 3, seed = 2)
attr(d3, "adjacency")                               # the true links
r3 <- rcausality(d3)
pl <- .pre("ext-placebo", placebo_test(r3, n_placebo = 199, reverse = TRUE, seed = 1))
pl
plot(pl)
```

The placebo runs find on average far fewer links than the data. The
time-reversed scores (TRGC) support the true links `v1 -> v2` and
`v3 -> v1` (and the indirect `v3 -> v2`), but not `v2 -> v1`, which the
pairwise analysis picks up from the feedback structure.

`robustness()` repeats the analysis with other lag orders, other
multiplicity corrections, contiguous subsamples and other methods:

```{r robust, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Robustness grid: green = the link is declared under the setting."}
rb <- .pre("ext-robust", robustness(r3, lags = 1:3, adjust = c("holm", "BH", "none"), n_sub = 20,
                                    methods = c("toda_yamamoto", "diks_panchenko", "te"), seed = 1))
rb
plot(rb)
```

# Forecasting with the detected links

The links of any method define a forecast model: every series is predicted
from its own lags and the lags of its causes, by the restricted VAR
(`model = "var"`), the Minnesota-prior VAR (`"bvar"`, for short series) or
random forests (`"rf"`, nonlinear). `forecast_compare()` selects the links
of every method on the training part only and compares the hold-out
one-step forecasts with those of the own-lags model (Diebold-Mariano
tests).

```{r fcmp, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Out-of-sample RMSE gain of the forecast models built from the links of each method, relative to the own-lags model."}
fcmp <- .pre("ext-fcmp", forecast_compare(d3, methods = c("granger", "bayes_granger", "toda_yamamoto", "te"),
                                          n_perm = 200, seed = 1))
fcmp
plot(fcmp)
```

```{r fc-bvar, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Forecasts of a short series from the Minnesota-prior model (posterior-predictive intervals)."}
ds <- sim_var(60, "x_to_y", seed = 2)
fb <- predict(rcausality(ds), h = 6, model = "bvar", n_sim = 500, holdout = 0.25)
fb
plot(fb, n_last = 30)
```

# Parallel computing

Every unit of work (a surrogate forest, a placebo data set, a panel unit,
an MCMC chain, a method of a comparison) receives its own L'Ecuyer-CMRG
random stream derived from the seed, so the results are identical for any
number of cores:

```{r par}
same <- .pre("ext-par", {
  if (.Platform$OS.type != "windows" && parallel::detectCores() >= 2) {
    t1 <- system.time(a <- placebo_test(r3, n_placebo = 200, seed = 7, cores = 1))[["elapsed"]]
    t2 <- system.time(b <- placebo_test(r3, n_placebo = 200, seed = 7, cores = 2))[["elapsed"]]
    list(identical = identical(a$links, b$links), seconds = c(`1 core` = t1, `2 cores` = t2))
  } else NULL
})
same
```

Diebold, F. X. and Mariano, R. S. (1995). Comparing predictive accuracy. *Journal of Business & Economic Statistics*, 13(3), 253-263.

Diks, C. and Panchenko, V. (2006). A new statistic and practical guidelines for nonparametric Granger causality testing. *Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control*, 30(9-10), 1647-1669.

Dumitrescu, E.-I. and Hurlin, C. (2012). Testing for Granger non-causality in heterogeneous panels. *Economic Modelling*, 29(4), 1450-1460.

Geweke, J. (1982). Measurement of linear dependence and feedback between multiple time series. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 77(378), 304-313.

Giannone, D., Lenza, M. and Primiceri, G. E. (2015). Prior selection for vector autoregressions. *The Review of Economics and Statistics*, 97(2), 436-451.

Haufe, S., Nikulin, V. V., Müller, K.-R. and Nolte, G. (2013). A critical assessment of connectivity measures for EEG data: a simulation study. *NeuroImage*, 64, 120-133.

Kosztyán, Z. T., Mátrai, R. and Kiss, D. (2026). Is the world getting smaller? Network-driven heterogeneity in gravity-model elasticities. *The World Economy*. doi:10.1111/twec.70148

Litterman, R. B. (1986). Forecasting with Bayesian vector autoregressions: five years of experience. *Journal of Business & Economic Statistics*, 4(1), 25-38.

Theiler, J., Eubank, S., Longtin, A., Galdrikian, B. and Farmer, J. D. (1992). Testing for nonlinearity in time series: the method of surrogate data. *Physica D*, 58, 77-94.
